power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Prolonged hospitalisation is an important burden among patients with sickle cell disease (SCD), with implications for healthcare utilisation and patient and caregiver burden.
Early prediction may support timely clinical and resource-management interventions.

Objective: To identify factors associated with prolonged hospitalisation among patients with SCD and compare the predictive performance of multivariable logistic regression with five supervised machine-learning algorithms.
Methods: This retrospective study included SCD inpatients aged ≥16 years admitted to the University of Ghana Hospital between January 2019 and December 2024.
Logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, support vector machine, and k-nearest neighbours models were developed using five-fold stratified cross-validation.
Class weighting and SMOTE were applied within training folds.
Model performance was evaluated using AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, and balanced accuracy.
Results: Among 872 patients, 137 (15.7%) experienced prolonged hospitalisation.

Acute chest syndrome (aOR=4.28; 95% CI: 2.31-7.94), malaria (aOR=3.77; 95% CI: 2.11-6.74), pneumonia (aOR=3.45; 95% CI: 2.02-5.90), and anaemia (aOR=2.71; 95% CI: 1.13-6.51) were independently associated with prolonged hospitalisation, whereas higher haemoglobin was protective (aOR=0.86; 95% CI: 0.78-0.96).
Logistic regression achieved the highest AUC-ROC (0.692), F1 score (0.418) and balanced accuracy (0.677), while random forest achieved the highest AUC-PR (0.375).
KNN had the highest sensitivity (59.3%) and XGBoost the highest specificity (87.2%).
AUC-ROC confidence intervals overlapped substantially across models.
46 Conclusion: Infection-related complications and anaemia were important predictors of prolonged 47 hospitalisation, while higher haemoglobin was protective.
ML models showed modest 48 performance without clear superiority over logistic regression.
Larger multicentre studies with 49 external validation are warranted.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) remains a major global health challenge as affected individuals experience a lifelong, severely disabling condition associated with reduced quality of life, high healthcare utilization, substantial economic burden and premature mortality (1, 2).
text.formatted: Sickle cell disease (SCD) remains a major global health challenge as affected individuals experience a lifelong, severely disabling condition associated with reduced quality of life, high healthcare utilization, substantial economic burden and premature mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: In 2021, an estimated 7.74 million people were living with SCD of which 515,000 were babies (2).
text.formatted: In 2021, an estimated 7.74 million people were living with SCD of which 515,000 were babies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref>.

text.text: Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly 80% of sickle cell disease births.
In the same year, SCD was responsible for approximately 376,000 deaths of which 81,100 occurred among children, making it the 12th leading cause of mortality globally (3).
text.formatted: In the same year, SCD was responsible for approximately 376,000 deaths of which 81,100 occurred among children, making it the 12th leading cause of mortality globally <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: It is the leading cause of death among children and adolescents in Sub-Saharan Africa (3).
text.formatted: It is the leading cause of death among children and adolescents in Sub-Saharan Africa <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Length of hospital stay (LOS) is a widely used proxy for disease severity, complication burden and healthcare resource utilisation (4).
text.formatted: Length of hospital stay (LOS) is a widely used proxy for disease severity, complication burden and healthcare resource utilisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Prolonged hospitalisation is associated with increased healthcare costs, greater risk of nosocomial complications, and substantial burden on patients and caregivers, making early identification of patients at risk of prolonged stay clinically and operationally valuable (5, 6).
text.formatted: Prolonged hospitalisation is associated with increased healthcare costs, greater risk of nosocomial complications, and substantial burden on patients and caregivers, making early identification of patients at risk of prolonged stay clinically and operationally valuable <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6)</ref>.

text.text: A recently published study in Ghana reported that 16% of SCD inpatients spent over 7 days in the hospital (7).
text.formatted: A recently published study in Ghana reported that 16% of SCD inpatients spent over 7 days in the hospital <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Multivariate logistic regression identified comorbidities, infection, acute chest syndrome, hyperhemolysis, sequestration crisis, and the need for transfusion as predictors of prolonged hospital stay among SCD inpatients (7).
text.formatted: Multivariate logistic regression identified comorbidities, infection, acute chest syndrome, hyperhemolysis, sequestration crisis, and the need for transfusion as predictors of prolonged hospital stay among SCD inpatients <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Traditional regression approaches like logistic regression, while interpretable, assume predominantly linear and additive relationships between predictors and outcome (8).
text.formatted: Traditional regression approaches like logistic regression, while interpretable, assume predominantly linear and additive relationships between predictors and outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: These may not capture higher-order interactions among clinical and haematological variables.

Supervised machine learning (ML) approaches offer potentially greater flexibility in modelling such relationships, though this must be weighed against reduced interpretability and, at modest sample sizes, a risk of overfitting (9).
text.formatted: Supervised machine learning (ML) approaches offer potentially greater flexibility in modelling such relationships, though this must be weighed against reduced interpretability and, at modest sample sizes, a risk of overfitting <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: This study therefore seeks to assess to identify the factors accounting for prolonged hospitalisation (>7 days) among SCD inpatients using multivariable logistic regression, and compare the predictive performance of five supervised ML algorithms against conventional logistic regression for this outcome.
text.formatted: This study therefore seeks to assess to identify the factors accounting for prolonged hospitalisation (>7 days) among SCD inpatients using multivariable logistic regression, and compare the predictive performance of five supervised ML algorithms against conventional logistic regression for this outcome.

text.text: This retrospective study analysed the medical records of patients diagnosed with sickle cell disease who were admitted to the University of Ghana Hospital.
Records of all SCD inpatients admitted between January 2019 and December 2024 were extracted from the Hospital Information System (HIS).

The extracted variables included demographic characteristics (age at admission and sex) and clinical characteristics, including acute chest syndrome, anaemia, malaria, pneumonia, and haemoglobin level.
Length of hospital stay was the primary outcome and was used to classify patients into non-prolonged (≤7 days) and prolonged hospitalisation (>7 days).
text.formatted: Length of hospital stay was the primary outcome and was used to classify patients into non-prolonged (≤7 days) and prolonged hospitalisation (>7 days).

text.text: Patients with a confirmed diagnosis of sickle cell disease (SCD) who were admitted as inpatients during the study period were eligible for inclusion.
The inclusion criteria were being aged 16 years or older and having documented admission and discharge dates from which length of hospital stay (LOS) could be determined.
Records of patients younger than 16 years was excluded.
Records with missing information on the outcome variable were also excluded.
Following these exclusions, 96 872 patients with complete data on all variables included in the analysis constituted the final 97 analytic sample.
Outcome Definition 101 The primary outcome was prolonged hospitalisation, defined a priori as a length of stay (LOS) 102 exceeding 7 days (7).
text.formatted: Outcome Definition 101 The primary outcome was prolonged hospitalisation, defined a priori as a length of stay (LOS) 102 exceeding 7 days <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Length of stay was defined as the number of days between the documented 103 date of admission and date of discharge.
Prediction was performed using clinical information 104 available within the first 48 hours of admission.
Candidate predictors comprised acute chest syndrome, anaemia, malaria, pneumonia, haemoglobin (Hb) and age at admission.
The variables were required to be supported by literature and available within the first 48 hours of admission to ensure that the model could theoretically be used for early risk stratification.
All variables were extracted from inpatient clinical records.
Binary variables were coded (present=1; absent=0).
Haemoglobin and age were retained as continuous variables.
The average VIF was 1.13 (min=1.00; max=1.09).
Given the observed outcome prevalence of 15.7%, class imbalance was addressed using class weighting and the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE).
These techniques were applied exclusively within training folds during cross-validation to avoid data leakage into validation/test partitions.
Continuous predictors were standardised (zero mean, unit variance) prior to fitting distance-based algorithms (support vector machine, k-nearest neighbours).

Five supervised classification algorithms were developed and compared: logistic regression (also serving as the interpretable clinical benchmark), random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), support vector machine (SVM) and k-nearest neighbours (KNN).
The models were developed and tuned using five-fold stratified cross-validation within the training set (80%) and subsequently evaluated on an independent held-out test set (20%).
Model hyperparameters were optimized using the grid search method.
Model discrimination was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC-PR).
The AUC-PR curve because of the class imbalance in the outcome.
Additional metrics reported include sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1-score and balanced accuracy.
Point estimates and 95% confidence intervals for key metrics were derived via bootstrap resampling (1,000 resamples) of the test-set predictions.

Permutation feature importance was computed for each algorithm to quantify the contribution of individual predictors to model discrimination (AUC-ROC) enabling comparison of predictor rankings across algorithms on a common scale.
Data were exported in CSV format and cleaned and coded using Microsoft Excel (version 2019).
The cleaned dataset was imported into Stata 14 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA) for statistical analysis.
Bivariate analyses were performed to examine differences in characteristics between patients with and without prolonged hospitalisation.
The independent-samples t test was used to compare continuous variables, while Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test was used to compare categorical variables, as appropriate.

The events-per-variable (EPV) ratio was approximately 23 (137 prolonged-hospitalisation events/6 candidate predictors) Machine learning model development, tuning and evaluation were conducted in Python [version 3.13] using scikit-learn, XGBoost, and imbalanced-learn packages in Google Colab.
This study utilized de-identified routine care data.
Ethical approval was obtained from the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research Institutional Review Board (NMIMR-IRB) (Study No.
The requirement for informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of de-identified data.
This study is reported in accordance with the TRIPOD+AI guideline for studies developing or validating multivariable prediction models.
A total of 872 SCD inpatients with complete data were included in the analysis.
Overall, 137 patients (15.7%; 95% CI: 13.4% to 18.2%) experienced prolonged hospitalization [Table 1].

text.text: Across models, a substantial proportion of patients with prolonged hospitalisation were incorrectly classified as having non-prolonged hospitalisation.
For example, the random forest model correctly identified 13 of the 27 patients with prolonged hospitalisation in the test set, corresponding to a sensitivity of 48.1%.

text.text: On the other hand, Acute chest syndrome (x=0.018; SD=0.014) and anaemia (x=0.006; 0.017) contributed comparatively The prevalence of prolonged hospitalisation in our facility was 15.7% (95% CI: 13.4% to 18.2%), meaning approximately one in six admissions stayed beyond 7 days.
This is comparable to the 16% reported at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH) in Ghana, although that study included patients aged ≥13 years (7).
text.formatted: This is comparable to the 16% reported at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH) in Ghana, although that study included patients aged ≥13 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: The similarity across two major Ghanaian hospitals suggests that prolonged admission is a consistent and substantial burden among patients with SCD, rather than a single-centre phenomenon.
However, direct comparison should be cautious because disease severity, genotype distribution and availability of specialist differ across the two health facilities.

The observed burden reinforces the need for effective interventions that prevents prolonged hospitalization among SCD patients; especially that prolonged hospitalization is linked with poor outcomes such as nosocomial infections, economic burden and caregiver-stress (5, 6, 10).
text.formatted: The observed burden reinforces the need for effective interventions that prevents prolonged hospitalization among SCD patients; especially that prolonged hospitalization is linked with poor outcomes such as nosocomial infections, economic burden and caregiver-stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>.

text.text: Acute chest syndrome (ACS) was significantly associated with increased odds of prolonged hospitalisation among patients with SCD.
This finding is consistent with the study in KATH that reported higher odds of prolonged hospitalisation among SCD patients with ACS (7).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with the study in KATH that reported higher odds of prolonged hospitalisation among SCD patients with ACS <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: ACS as a severe, acute lung injury, prolongs hospitalization because its management typically necessitates aggressive oxygen therapy, blood transfusions and intensive monitoring before a patient reaches clinical stability.
Patients with pneumonia were 3.5 times more likely to experience a prolonged hospital stay compared with patients without pneumonia.

The association with pneumonia is clinically plausible because pulmonary infection can worsen hypoxemia and systemic inflammation, thereby promoting erythrocyte sickling and vaso-occlusive complications (11).
text.formatted: The association with pneumonia is clinically plausible because pulmonary infection can worsen hypoxemia and systemic inflammation, thereby promoting erythrocyte sickling and vaso-occlusive complications <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, treating pneumonia requires prolonged antimicrobial therapy, respiratory support and close clinical monitoring, all of which extend the time to recovery.
Having malaria increased the SCD patients' odds for prolonged hospitalization by 3.8 times, compared with patients without malaria.

This finding aligns with the broader clinical consensus that malaria acts as a severe pathological catalyst in individuals with homozygous sickle cell anaemia, triggering acute haemolytic crises, worsening baseline chronic anaemia, and precipitating vaso-occlusive events (12).
text.formatted: This finding aligns with the broader clinical consensus that malaria acts as a severe pathological catalyst in individuals with homozygous sickle cell anaemia, triggering acute haemolytic crises, worsening baseline chronic anaemia, and precipitating vaso-occlusive events <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Because malaria infection promotes systemic inflammation and microvascular sludging, patients frequently develop severe multisystem complications that require extended antimalarial therapy, intensive hydration, and frequent blood transfusions, thereby prolonging their hospital course.
Anaemia was a significant predictor of prolonged hospitalisation in our cohort, likely reflecting low haemoglobin as a marker of severe SCD rather than an isolated cause.
Consistent with Ershler et al. (2023), anaemia may initiate a cascade of complications and greater healthcare utilisation(13).

Each 1 g/dL increase in haemoglobin was associated with a 14% reduction in the odds of prolonged hospitalisation, suggesting haemoglobin is a useful indicator of disease burden and clinical stability.
These findings support monitoring and optimising haemoglobin in hospitalised patients with SCD.
The traditional and machine-learning models demonstrated modest predictive performance with no clear differences in discrimination.

The comparable performance of logistic regression may reflect predominantly linear predictor-outcome relationships and the small number of predictors under which more complex algorithms may offer limited incremental benefit(14).

Under such condition, logistic regression provides a pragmatic and interpretable approach for risk stratification, while alternative algorithms may be preferable when sensitivity, specificity, or minority-class discrimination is prioritized.
There are limitations worth sharing.
First, this was a retrospective, single-centre study, which may limit generalisability to other settings.
Second, the sample size (n=872) is modest for ML model development, particularly for the minority class(n=137).
Third, potentially relevant predictor like socioeconomic status was not available and may confound or mediate the associations observed.

The multivariate logistic regression indicates that infection-related complications (acute chest syndrome, malaria, pneumonia) and anaemia severity are key independent determinants of prolonged hospitalisation among SCD inpatients in this malaria-endemic cohort while higher haemoglobin was protective.
Supervised ML algorithms offered modest, and not clearly superior, discrimination compared with conventional logistic regression at this sample size.

These findings support infection prevention and haemoglobin optimisation as potential targets for reducing prolonged hospitalisation, and highlight the need for larger and externally validated studies before predictive models are considered for clinical use.
